reference_rockets.name: Redstone-class
reference_rockets.description: A single-stage alcohol/LOX rocket carrying a small crewed capsule on a suborbital hop.

geometry_notes.overall: Real Mercury-Redstone: about 25.4 m tall including capsule and escape tower, 1.78 m (70 in) diameter, about 30,000 kg (66,000 lb) at liftoff. Here: tower 4.5 + capsule 2.9 + booster 18.0 = 25.4 m; liftoff mass 29,900 kg.
geometry_notes.nose: The capsule itself is the nose. Modelled as a 2.9 m cone weighing 1,300 kg (real capsule about 1,300 kg at launch; it was a blunt truncated cone, not a pointed one).
geometry_notes.payload: The adapter plus instrument compartment between capsule and tanks. Length and mass are ESTIMATES.
geometry_notes.body: Tank section. 12.0 m length is an ESTIMATE (18.0 m booster minus the instrument and tail sections). Propellant 23,600 kg is DERIVED from 350 kN / (215 s x g0) = 166 kg/s times the real 142 s burn. Dry mass 3,000 kg is an ESTIMATE chosen so total liftoff mass matches about 30 t.
geometry_notes.engine: Same numbers as engines.json 'redstone_class' (inspired by the Rocketdyne A-7: 78,000 lbf sea-level thrust). Tail section length 3.5 m is an ESTIMATE.
geometry_notes.fins: Count 4 is real. Span 1.07 m per fin is DERIVED from a roughly 3.9 m overall fin span. Root chord, tip chord, sweep and mass are ESTIMATES from drawings, not sourced numbers.
geometry_notes.options: The real Redstone steered with carbon jet vanes in the exhaust plus air rudders, not a gimbal; 'gimballed: true' stands in for that active steering. Escape tower mass and length are ESTIMATES. The tower's aerodynamics are ignored; only its mass counts.

real_flight.notes: Apogee, range, speed and duration are from memory of the NASA MR-3 mission summary: VERIFY. max_q_pa (about 575 lb/ft2) is LOW CONFIDENCE and may be wrong. Mercury-Redstone 4 (21 July 1961) reached about 190 km and 486 km downrange.

reference_rockets.source: Inspired by the real Mercury-Redstone Launch Vehicle (NASA MSFC, 1960-61). See 'The Mercury-Redstone Project' (NASA TMX-53107, 1964) and 'This New Ocean' (NASA SP-4201) for the numbers to verify against.

optional_upper_stage.source: MADE UP: same as the presets.json 'big' upper stage. The real Mercury-Redstone had no upper stage; the Redstone-derived Jupiter-C / Juno I carried small solid-rocket upper stages instead.

reference_rockets.name: Juno-class
reference_rockets.description: A stretched Redstone-class booster carrying a spinning tub of small solid rockets in three stages (11, then 3, then 1), the way Juno I put the 14 kg Explorer 1 into orbit in 1958.

geometry_notes.overall: Real Juno I (Jupiter-C, 1958): about 21 m tall, 1.78 m diameter, about 29 t at liftoff. A Redstone with stretched tanks, then a spinning tub of scaled-down Sergeant solid rockets: 11 in stage 2, 3 in stage 3, 1 in stage 4 (which stayed attached to Explorer 1).
geometry_notes.nose: Explorer 1's own nose. Its mass is counted in the 14 kg payload, so the nose segment weighs 0 here. Length 0.5 m is an ESTIMATE.
geometry_notes.body: Tank length 14.4 m is an ESTIMATE: the Redstone-class reference's 12 m plus about 2.4 m of stretch. Propellant 25,700 kg is DERIVED like the Redstone's: 350 kN / (215 s x g0) = 166 kg/s times an ESTIMATED 155 s burn. Dry mass 3,000 kg is an ESTIMATE (same as the Redstone-class, the stretch roughly offset by the lighter instrument section).
geometry_notes.engine: The Redstone-class engine with the same numbers as engines.json (350 kN sea level, 382.6 kN vacuum, Isp 215 s / 235 s, 700 kg). The real Jupiter-C burned hydyne for a little more thrust; that uprate is deliberately NOT modelled.
geometry_notes.fins: Same ESTIMATED fins as the Redstone-class reference.
geometry_notes.options: Gimballed stands in for the real carbon jet vanes, like the Redstone-class reference.
geometry_notes.upper_stages: Each motor is an ESTIMATE of a 1950s 'Baby Sergeant': 7.3 kN for about 6.5 s, Isp 220 s, about 22 kg of propellant in a 4.7 kg case, 1.22 m long, 0.152 m wide. 220 s is typical of 1950s polysulfide / ammonium perchlorate solids. Stage structure (the spinning tub and its rings) is an ESTIMATE.

real_flight.notes: From memory: VERIFY against NASA/JPL records. Explorer 1 (with its attached fourth-stage case) weighed about 14 kg and reached roughly 358 x 2,550 km. The real ascent lofted the tub to about 360 km and fired the solids near-horizontally at apogee.

reference_rockets.source: Inspired by the real Juno I / Jupiter-C launch vehicle (Army Ballistic Missile Agency and JPL, 1958). Every number is an estimate: see geometry_notes. VERIFY against NASA SP-4201-era sources and JPL's Explorer 1 records.

optional_upper_stages.source: ESTIMATE: 11 motors x 22 kg propellant; 30 kg of tub structure is a guess.
ESTIMATE: 3 motors x 22 kg propellant; 8 kg of ring structure is a guess.
ESTIMATE: 1 motor x 22 kg propellant, attached to the satellite; 1 kg of fittings is a guess.
